Bolt vs. Screw: Four Primary Criteria The four primary criteria are based on the root of the two definitions above. Each of the four criteria essentially attempts to confirm a key element of one definition or the other. If a part in question clearly satisfies any of the four criteria, it can be identified without any further examination. These are classified as bolts because you can’t turn the head during assembly. Criterion 1 — Bolt If the fastener in question has a head or other design feature that prevents turning during assembly and which can be tightened only by turning a nut, then the fastener is a bolt. This criterion is a process of elimination. Screws are designed to be tightened by turning the head, so if you can’t turn the head, the part must be a bolt. Criterion Two — Bolt If an externally threaded fastener has an intended function that requires it to be assembled with a nut, then the fastener is a bolt.

Analyzing the Difference Between Bolts and Screws Fastener Mechanics and Load Paths: The structural performance of bolts relies on axial pre-tension to clamp joint members together, whereas screws transfer loads primarily through direct thread shear engagement with the host material. To truly understand the difference, we must look at how they handle mechanical stress. A bolt is designed to act as a spring. When you tighten a bolt-nut assembly, you stretch the bolt within its elastic limit. This stretch creates a clamping force that holds the two mating surfaces together. The friction between these surfaces is what actually carries the shear load in a friction-grip joint. Thread Design and Pitch Variations Thread Geometry Standards: Bolts feature uniform, fine or coarse machine threads designed to mate with nuts, whereas screws utilize tapered, sharper threads designed to cut or form their own mating threads in the substrate. Screws typically have a more aggressive thread pitch. This allows them to grip the surrounding material tightly.
